To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
EphB2 and EphB4 are expressed in hippocampal neurons, and that they are involved in the regulation of dendritic spine morphology and synaptic transmission in the hippocampus.
EphB receptors and FAK regulate dendritic spine morphology and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus.
EphB1/2/4 receptor tyrosine kinases are expressed in the hippocampus, where EphB1/4 are enriched in the postsynaptic compartment of dendritic spines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which EphB receptors regulate dendritic spine morphology and function.
the role of ephrins and Eph receptors in the development of the nervous system.
the role of Eph receptor signaling in dendritic spine morphogenesis, and the underlying molecular mechanism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EphB2 is a key molecule for the development of dendritic spines and that it is involved in the regulation of spine morphologies and spine density in the adult brain.
EphB4 is a key regulator in the development and maintenance of dendritic spine morphology, but the underlying mechanisms remain to be elucidated.
the EphB4 receptor plays an essential role in the regulation of dendritic spine morphology and synaptic plasticity, and that it may be a potential target in the treatment of mental disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EphB receptors and their ligands are important regulators of dendritic spine morphology, and that they do so by regulating focal adhesion kinase.
EphB maintains spine morphology through FAK, and that this function is independent of EphB's known roles in cell migration, axon guidance, and synapse development.

EphB maintains dendritic spine morphology through focal adhesion kinase (FAK), which is a critical regulator for the maintenance of dendritic spine structure and function, and that FAK regulates dendritic spine morphology in an ephrinB-dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we have identified a mechanism by which EphB receptor tyrosine kinases can regulate the structure of dendritic spines and synapses, and we have shown that the mechanism involves the focal adhesion kinase (FAK).
EphB signaling maintains spine morphology through FAK.

EphB receptors maintain the morphology of dendritic spines by activating FAK, and that FAK is a key regulator of spine morphology and synaptic plasticity, says lead investigator, Dr. Michael Froemke, Assistant Professor at the Feil Family Brain and Mind Research Institute at Weill Cornell Medical College, New York.
